title: Find low-stock products in a Shopify CSV with 60 lines of Python
author: BotHot
summary: If you run a small shop, you probably export your products from Shopify now and then. Somewhere in that file are the variants that are almost sold out, and scrolling through a spreadsheet to find them is boring and easy to get wrong. This small script reads a Shopify product export and lists every variant at or below a stock threshold. It only reads the file and never changes it. It uses nothing but Python's standard library. What the export looks like Shopify's product CSV has one row per variant. Products with several images get extra rows that only contain an image URL, so the quantity cell is empty there. The columns we need are: Handle (the product ID in the URL) Title (only filled on the first row of a product) Variant SKU Variant Inventory Qty The script #!/usr/bin/env python3 import argparse import csv import sys QTY_COLUMN = " Variant Inventory Qty " SKU_COLUMN = " Variant SKU " HANDLE_COLUMN = " Handle " TITLE_COLUMN = " Title " def read_rows ( path ): with open ( path , newline = "" , encoding = " utf-8-sig " ) as f : reader = csv . DictReader ( f ) missing = [ c for c in ( HANDLE_COLUMN , QTY_COLUMN ) if c not in ( reader . fieldnames or [])] if missing : sys . exit ( f " Missing column(s): { ' , ' . join ( missing ) } " ) return list ( reader ) def find_low_stock ( rows , threshold ): low , unreadable = [], [] last_title = {} for number , row in enumerate ( rows , start = 2 ): # row 1 is the header handle = row [ HANDLE_COLUMN ] if row . get ( TITLE_COLUMN ): last_title [ handle ] = row [ TITLE_COLUMN ] raw = ( row . get ( QTY_COLUMN ) or "" ). strip () if raw == "" : continue # extra image rows have no quantity try : qty = int ( float ( raw )) except ValueError : unreadable . append (( number , handle , raw )) continue if qty <= threshold : low . append ({ " row " : number , " handle " : handle , " title " : last_title . get ( handle , "" ), " sku " : row . get ( SKU_COLUMN , "" ), " qty " : qty , }) return low , unreadable def main (): parser = argparse . ArgumentParser () parser . add_argument ( " csv_file " ) parser . add_argument ( " --threshold " , type = int , default = 5 ) parser . add_argument ( " --out " , default = " low_stock.csv " ) args = parser . parse_args () rows = read_rows ( args . csv_file ) low , unreadable = find_low_stock ( rows , args . threshold ) with open ( args . out , " w " , newline = "" , encoding = " utf-8 " ) as f : writer = csv . DictWriter ( f , fieldnames = [ " row " , " handle " , " title " , " sku " , " qty " ]) writer . writeheader () writer . writerows ( sorted ( low , key = lambda r : r [ " qty " ])) print ( f " { len ( rows ) } rows read, { len ( low ) } at or below { args . threshold } " ) for r in sorted ( low , key = lambda r : r [ " qty " ]): print ( f " qty { r [ ' qty ' ] : > 3 } { r [ ' sku ' ] or ' - ' : < 10 } { r [ ' title ' ] or r [ ' handle ' ] } " ) for number , handle , raw in unreadable : print ( f " row { number } : cannot read quantity { raw !r} ( { handle } ) " ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : main () Trying it I tested it on a small made-up file (not real shop data): Handle,Title,Variant SKU,Variant Inventory Qty,Image Src blue-mug,Blue Mug,MUG-B,12,https://example.com/a.jpg blue-mug,,,,https://example.com/b.jpg red-mug,Red Mug,MUG-R,3,https://example.com/c.jpg tote-bag,Tote Bag,BAG-1,0,https://example.com/d.jpg sticker-pack,Sticker Pack,STK-1,five,https://example.com/e.jpg poster-a3,Poster A3,POS-A3,5,https://example.com/f.jpg notebook,Notebook,NB-1,40,https://example.com/g.jpg $ python3 low_stock.py sample.csv --threshold 5 7 rows read, 3 at or below 5 qty 0 BAG-1 Tote Bag qty 3 MUG-R Red Mug qty 5 POS-A3 Poster A3 row 6: cannot read quantity 'five' (sticker-pack) The sticker pack has a typo ( five instead of 5 ). The script does not guess; it reports the row number so you can fix it. The empty image row of the blue mug is skipped on purpose. With --threshold 2 only the tote bag is listed. The file low_stock.csv contains the same list, sorted from lowest to highest stock, ready to open in Excel. Notes and limits It checks the quantity column only. If a variant does not track inventory, Shopify leaves that cell empty and the variant is skipped. The threshold is a plain number. A product that sells ten a day needs a different threshold than one that sells one a month, so adjust it per shop. Check the column names in your own export. Shopify has changed its export format before, and the script stops with a clear message if a column is missing. If you want to extend it, an easy next step is a second threshold per product type, or sending the result by e-mail once a week. title: Getting Started With Python Web Scraping: Tools, Tips & Code
author: Alina Shah
summary:
Have you ever wanted to collect product prices from multiple websites, track job listings, or gather article titles without copying everything manually? That is where Python web scraping comes in. Instead of opening dozens of pages and transferring information into a spreadsheet, you can write a script to retrieve web pages, extract the information you need, and organize it into a usable format. The tricky part is that websites don't all store information the same way. Some use straightforward HTML, while others load content with JavaScript, block automated requests, or change their page structure without warning. In this guide, I will walk through essential Python web scraping tools , show working code examples, and explain how to build easier-to-maintain scrapers. What Is Python Web Scraping? Python web scraping is the process of using Python code to retrieve information from web pages and extract specific data from their content. For example, suppose you want to collect: Product names and prices from a permitted product listing page. Job titles and company names from public job listings. Article headlines and publication dates from a news archive. Publicly available research data from a website. Links and metadata from a directory of resources. You could copy the information manually, but that becomes inefficient when you need hundreds of records or want to repeat the process regularly. A scraper automates the workflow: Send a request to a web page. Receive the page content. Parse the HTML. Identify the elements containing the information. Extract and clean the values. Save the results to a file or database. Python is a popular choice because its libraries make HTTP requests, HTML parsing, browser automation, and data processing relatively straightforward. The Best Python Web Scraping Tools to Know You do not need a complicated stack to start scraping. The tools you choose should depend on how the target website delivers its content. 1. Requests: Retrieve Web Pages The Requests library sends HTTP requests and provides a convenient way to access responses. It is a good starting point when the information you need is already present in the page's HTML. Install it with: pip install requests A basic example: import requests url = " https://example.com " response = requests . get ( url , timeout = 15 ) response . raise_for_status () print ( response . status_code ) print ( response . text [: 500 ]) The get() method requests the page. The timeout prevents the request from waiting indefinitely, while raise_for_status() raises an exception for unsuccessful HTTP responses. For real projects, handle network errors and timeouts instead of assuming every request will succeed. 2. Beautiful Soup: Extract Information From HTML A successful HTTP request does not automatically give you clean data. The response usually contains HTML with headings, links, paragraphs, navigation, and other elements. Beautiful Soup helps you parse that HTML and select the elements you need. Install it: pip install beautifulsoup4 Let's extract the title and headings from a page: import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup url = " https://example.com " response = requests . get ( url , timeout = 15 ) response . raise_for_status () soup = BeautifulSoup ( response . text , " html.parser " ) page_title = ( soup . title . get_text ( strip = True ) if soup . title else " No title found " ) print ( " Page title: " , page_title ) for heading in soup . find_all ([ " h1 " , " h2 " ]): print ( heading . get_text ( " " , strip = True )) This example demonstrates two useful techniques: checking whether an element exists before accessing it and using get_text() to remove the HTML markup from the extracted content. Beautiful Soup is especially useful for small and medium scraping tasks involving predictable HTML. 3. lxml: Parse HTML Efficiently The lxml library is another option for parsing HTML and XML. It supports XPath expressions, which can be useful when you need to select elements using more detailed structural rules. Install it with: pip install lxml You can use it directly with BeautifulSoup: from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """

Python Web Scraping

A beginner ' s guide

""" soup = BeautifulSoup ( html , " lxml " ) heading = soup . find ( " h1 " ) summary = soup . select_one ( " .summary " ) print ( heading . get_text ( strip = True )) print ( summary . get_text ( strip = True )) For many beginners, Beautiful Soup with Python's built-in HTML parser is enough. Consider lxml when you need XPath or want to evaluate parsing performance for a larger workload. 4. Scrapy: Build Larger Scraping Projects Scrapy is a more complete framework for crawling websites and extracting data across multiple pages. It provides request scheduling, item processing, pipelines, and result exporting. Install it: pip install scrapy Create a project: scrapy startproject my_scraper Scrapy becomes useful when a project needs to follow pagination, visit many links, manage retries, and process a substantial number of records. For a single page, it may be unnecessary. For a recurring crawl with several stages, its built-in structure can save time compared with writing everything from scratch. 5. Playwright: Handle JavaScript-Rendered Pages Some websites display their main content only after JavaScript runs. A simple Requests call may return an HTML shell without the data you expected. Playwright automates a browser, allowing you to wait for page content and interact with elements when permitted. Install it: pip install playwright playwright install chromium Example: from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright with sync_playwright () as p : browser = p . chromium . launch ( headless = True ) page = browser . new_page () page . goto ( " https://example.com " , wait_until = " domcontentloaded " ) page_title = page . title () print ( page_title ) browser . close () This example opens a page in a browser and retrieves its title. If you need content loaded later by JavaScript, wait for a specific, documented page element rather than adding an arbitrary long delay. Browser automation consumes more resources than a basic HTTP request, so use it only when the target page actually requires it. A Complete Python Web Scraping Example Let's combine Requests and Beautiful Soup into a small scraper. For this example, we will use Books to Scrape , a demonstration website intended for scraping practice. The script retrieves book titles and prices from its first catalog page. Install the dependencies: pip install requests beautifulsoup4 Then create a Python file named scrape_books.py : import csv import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup URL = " https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-1.html " HEADERS = { " User-Agent " : " LearningScraper/1.0 " } def scrape_books (): response = requests . get ( URL , headers = HEADERS , timeout = 15 ) response . raise_for_status () soup = BeautifulSoup ( response . text , " html.parser " ) books = [] for item in soup . select ( " article.product_pod " ): title_element = item . select_one ( " h3 a " ) price_element = item . select_one ( " .price_color " ) if title_element is None or price_element is None : continue books . append ({ " title " : title_element . get ( " title " , "" ). strip (), " price " : price_element . get_text ( strip = True ) }) return books def save_to_csv ( books ): with open ( " books.csv " , " w " , newline = "" , encoding = " utf-8 " ) as file : writer = csv . DictWriter ( file , fieldnames = [ " title " , " price " ] ) writer . writeheader () writer . writerows ( books ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : books = scrape_books () save_to_csv ( books ) print ( f " Saved { len ( books ) } books to books.csv " ) for book in books [: 5 ]: print ( book ) Run the script: python scrape_books.py If the request succeeds and the page structure matches the selectors, the script creates a books.csv file containing the extracted titles and prices. How the Code Works Step 1: Request the page. Requests downloads the HTML from the catalog URL. Step 2: Parse the HTML. Beautiful Soup converts the response into a structure that Python can search. Step 3: Find book listings. The CSS selector article.product_pod targets each book card. Step 4: Extract fields. The script retrieves the book title from the link's title attribute and the displayed price from the price element. Step 5: Save the results. Python's built-in csv module writes the records to a spreadsheet-friendly file. The script also checks whether the expected elements exist. This matters because a missing element should not crash the entire scraping process unnecessarily. The example is deliberately limited to one page. A production scraper would need additional handling for pagination, unexpected page layouts, network failures, and website changes. How to Choose the Right Python Scraping Tool Use this quick guide when deciding which library to start with. Tool Best use case Learning curve Requests Downloading HTML Low Beautiful Soup Extracting text, links, and attributes Low lxml HTML/XML parsing and XPath Low to moderate Scrapy Multi-page crawling and structured scraping pipelines Moderate Playwright Pages that require browser rendering or interaction Moderate For a first project, I would start with Requests and Beautiful Soup. They cover most straightforward scraping tasks without adding unnecessary complexity. Move to Scrapy when the project grows into a crawler. Use Playwright when you confirm that the information depends on browser execution or interaction. Practical Tips for More Reliable Web Scraping A script that works once is not necessarily a reliable scraper. Small changes to the website, network conditions, or response format can break it. 1. Check the Website's Rules First Before collecting data, review the website's terms, applicable policies, and robots.txt guidance. Prefer an official API or permitted data export when available. Do not assume that publicly visible information is automatically free to collect or reuse. Respect access restrictions, copyright, privacy requirements, and rate limits. Do not bypass authentication, CAPTCHAs, or other technical controls without authorization. 2. Add Timeouts and Error Handling Network requests can fail because of timeouts, DNS problems, server errors, or temporary connectivity issues. A simple pattern is: import requests try : response = requests . get ( " https://example.com " , timeout = 15 ) response . raise_for_status () except requests . exceptions . Timeout : print ( " The request timed out. " ) except requests . exceptions . HTTPError as error : print ( f " HTTP error: { error } " ) except requests . exceptions . RequestException as error : print ( f " Request failed: { error } " ) For recurring jobs, record errors in logs and decide which failures are safe to retry. Respect server-provided rate-limit information and avoid retrying indefinitely. 3. Use Specific CSS Selectors Broad selectors can collect unrelated information. For example, selecting every paragraph may capture navigation labels, advertisements, and footer text. Inspect the page's HTML and target the elements that correspond to the data you actually need. When possible, use stable attributes or semantic elements. Avoid depending on automatically generated CSS class names that may change frequently. 4. Handle Missing and Inconsistent Data Not every record will contain every field. Prices might be missing, publication dates might use different formats, or a page might have an unexpected layout. Check for missing elements before extracting values. Normalize whitespace, dates, and numbers, and validate the resulting data before saving it. If the output will feed a dashboard or database, add tests for the fields that must always be present. 5. Avoid Sending Too Many Requests High request volumes can overload a website and cause your IP address to be blocked. Keep request rates reasonable, follow published limits, and cache responses when appropriate. For a small sequential scraper, even a short delay between requests may help reduce unnecessary load: import time for url in permitted_urls : # Fetch and process the page here. time . sleep ( 1 ) This is a basic pacing example, not a guarantee that one request per second is permitted. Follow the target site's actual requirements. 6. Keep Scraped Data Separate From Your Code Save collected records to CSV, JSON, or a database instead of mixing data extraction with every downstream task. This makes it easier to inspect the results, rerun analysis without downloading the pages again, and identify whether a problem occurred during retrieval, parsing, or storage. For recurring projects, record when the data was collected and where it came from. This provides useful context when values change. Common Python Web Scraping Problems and Fixes The script returns an empty list: Check the page source and confirm that your CSS selectors match the actual HTML. The data might be loaded through JavaScript, or the page may have returned an error message instead of the expected content. The request returns a 403 or 429 response: The server may be denying access or enforcing rate limits. Review the site's rules and reduce request frequency where appropriate. Do not attempt to bypass access controls. The extracted text contains extra whitespace: Use methods such as get_text(" ", strip=True) and normalize the values before saving them. The scraper stops when one element is missing: Check for None before accessing an element's attributes or methods, and log records that do not match the expected structure. The scraper becomes slow: Avoid launching a browser for pages that work with HTTP requests. For larger crawls, consider Scrapy's request scheduling and concurrency controls, configured to respect the target website's limits. The website changes its layout: Add tests that verify important selectors and expected fields. When a scraper runs regularly, monitor record counts and unexpected missing values so structural changes do not go unnoticed. When Should You Use an API Instead of Web Scraping? Web scraping is not always the best solution. If a website provides an official API, that is usually the first option to investigate. An API typically provides structured responses, documented fields, and clearer expectations about access and rate limits. Scraping may be useful when the information is available only in HTML, and you are permitted to collect it. Before building a scraper, ask three questions: Is there an official API or downloadable dataset? Am I permitted to access, collect, and use this information? Can I maintain the scraper if the page structure changes? If an API provides the data you need, it may be more reliable and easier to maintain than parsing HTML. Conclusion Python web scraping is a practical way to automate data collection, whether you are learning to extract a few headlines or building a recurring data pipeline. Requests and Beautiful Soup are excellent starting points for ordinary HTML pages, while lxml, Scrapy, and Playwright address more specialized needs. The biggest lesson is to keep the first project simple. Choose one permitted page, inspect its HTML, extract a small set of fields, and save the results to CSV. Once that works, add error handling, validation, logging, and sensible request limits. Reliable scraping is not just about getting data out of a page. It is about collecting the right information responsibly and building a script that keeps working when conditions change. FAQs Is Python good for web scraping? Yes. Python has libraries for HTTP requests, HTML parsing, browser automation, crawling, and data processing. Beginners can start with Requests and Beautiful Soup, then use tools such as Scrapy or Playwright when their requirements become more complex. Which Python library is best for web scraping? Beautiful Soup is a good choice for extracting information from HTML, usually alongside Requests. Scrapy suits larger crawling projects, while Playwright is useful when content requires browser rendering or interaction. Can Python scrape JavaScript websites? Yes, but the right method depends on how the website delivers its content. If the data is available through a permitted underlying API or in the initial HTML, a normal HTTP request may be enough. If the page requires browser-side JavaScript, a tool such as Playwright can render it. Is web scraping legal? It depends on the website, the data, the access method, and the intended use. Review the site's terms, access rules, privacy obligations, and applicable laws. Public visibility alone does not establish permission to collect or reuse all content. How do I save scraped data in Python? You can save scraped records to CSV using Python's built-in csv module or to JSON using the json module. For larger or recurring projects, a database may be a better fit.

title: Downloading an Alibaba supplier's whole catalog as JSON (and vetting suppliers with it)
author: Gio Rich
summary: I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify with a free trial credit. Searching Alibaba shows you products from hundreds of suppliers. Once you have a shortlist, the useful question flips: what else does this supplier sell, how focused is the catalog, which of their products actually sell, what is certified, and is the company behind it a 140-person factory or an 8-person trading office? That answer lives on the supplier's storefront ( name.en.alibaba.com ), 16 products per page, often 30 to 80 pages deep. Copying that by hand gets old fast, so I wrote Alibaba Supplier Store Scraper to turn a store URL, a product URL or a keyword into one clean JSON row per product, over plain HTTP. This post covers how it works, calling it from Python and Node, what a row looks like, and a small project: scoring suppliers from their catalogs. How it works A supplier storefront page server-renders its modules as URL-encoded JSON inside module-data attributes: the supplier card, the store's own category tree, and the product list with paging. The actor decodes those, maps each product card to flat fields (price range, MOQ, certificates, sold in the last 180 days, orders, ready-to-ship, store category with its parent) and copies the supplier card onto every row: business type, supplier identity, years on Alibaba, verified staff count, store rating, the inspection company that verified it, ranking badges, main products and capability tags such as "ODM services available" or "Patents awarded (6)". No contact person names, phones or emails are collected. After page 1 it knows the product count, so it queues exactly the pages it needs and reads them in parallel. Give it a product URL and it finds the supplier on the product page first; give it a keyword and it uses the JSON endpoint Alibaba's own search page calls to collect the suppliers behind the results. A keyword inside each store, ready-to-ship only, and price / MOQ filters are applied before anything is charged. It connects directly and only retries blocked requests through a proxy. Calling it from Python from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( " <YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN> " ) run = client . actor ( " rel8ble/alibaba-supplier-store-scraper " ). call ( run_input = { " storeUrls " : [ " https://alextechnology.en.alibaba.com/ " , " https://www.alibaba.com/product-detail/High-Quality-PU-Yoga-Mat-Custom_1601669249206.html " , ], " searchTerms " : [ " bluetooth speaker " ], " maxStoresPerSearch " : 3 , " maxProductsPerStore " : 50 , }) for p in client . dataset ( run [ " defaultDatasetId " ]). iterate_items (): print ( p [ " supplierName " ][: 30 ], " | " , p [ " storeCategory " ], " | " , p [ " priceText " ], " | MOQ " , p [ " moq " ], " | sold " , p [ " soldLast180Days " ]) The same from Node: import { ApifyClient } from ' apify-client ' ; const client = new ApifyClient ({ token : ' <YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN> ' }); const run = await client . actor ( ' rel8ble/alibaba-supplier-store-scraper ' ). call ({ storeUrls : [ ' alextechnology ' ], keywordInStore : ' earphone ' , readyToShipOnly : true , maxProductsPerStore : 0 , // the whole matching catalog }); const { items } = await client . dataset ( run . defaultDatasetId ). listItems (); console . log ( items . length , ' ready-to-ship earphones from ' , items [ 0 ]?. supplierName ); What a row looks like From a real run, trimmed: { "productId" : "1601240924267" , "title" : "HM11 Retro Bluetooth Speaker, Vintage Decor, Mini Wireless Bluetooth Speaker, Fashion Style Outdoor Accessories" , "priceMin" : 3.89 , "priceMax" : 4.49 , "moq" : 2 , "moqUnit" : "pieces" , "readyToShip" : true , "certificates" : [ "FCC" , "DECLARATION OF CONFORMITY" ], "soldLast180Days" : 4 , "orderCount" : 3 , "storeCategory" : "Bluetooth Speaker" , "supplierName" : "Shenzhen Yuzhuo Technology Co., Ltd." , "supplierBusinessType" : [ "Trading Company" ], "supplierIdentity" : "Multispecialty Supplier" , "supplierYearsOnAlibaba" : 13 , "supplierStaffCount" : 8 , "supplierRating" : 4.4 , "supplierVerifiedBy" : "SGS Group" , "supplierCapabilities" : [ "Registered trademarks (3)" , "Patents awarded (2)" , "ODM services available" ], "storeTotalProducts" : 271 , "source" : "search" , "searchTerm" : "bluetooth speaker" } Project: scoring suppliers from their catalogs A supplier that sells yoga mats, mouse pads and flower pots is a different partner from one with 300 listings in a single category. With one run you can measure that: from collections import Counter , defaultdict rows = list ( client . dataset ( run [ " defaultDatasetId " ]). iterate_items ()) by_store = defaultdict ( list ) for r in rows : by_store [ r [ " storeUrl " ]]. append ( r ) print ( f " { ' supplier ' : 32 } { ' focus ' : > 5 } { ' certs ' : > 5 } { ' selling ' : > 7 } { ' staff ' : > 5 } { ' years ' : > 5 } type " ) for store , items in by_store . items (): s = items [ 0 ] top_cat = Counter (( i [ " storeCategory " ] or "" ). split ( " > " )[ 0 ] for i in items ). most_common ( 1 )[ 0 ][ 1 ] focus = top_cat / len ( items ) # share of products in the biggest category certified = sum ( bool ( i [ " certificates " ]) for i in items ) / len ( items ) selling = sum ( i [ " soldLast180Days " ] > 0 or i [ " orderCount " ] > 0 for i in items ) / len ( items ) print ( f " { s [ ' supplierName ' ][ : 32 ] : 32 } { focus : 5.0 % } { certified : 5.0 % } { selling : 7.0 % } " f " { s [ ' supplierStaffCount ' ] or ' - ' : > 5 } { s [ ' supplierYearsOnAlibaba ' ] or ' - ' : > 5 } { ' / ' . join ( s [ ' supplierBusinessType ' ]) } " ) Focus, certification share and the share of listings with real sales are three quick signals you cannot get from search results alone. Pass the url of the products that survive to a detail scraper when you need full price ladders and lead times. Pricing and limits $1.50 per 1,000 products, no start fee. Products skipped by filters, duplicates, missing stores and failed requests are never charged. This is listing-level data: full quantity ladders, SKUs and specs are on product pages. Sales counts show on about a third of products in my tests; supplier rating, years, business type and verification on every row. Up to 4,000 products per store (scrape by category or keyword for bigger ones). title: Five rich-text editors, five ways to inject text, and the layer that actually matters
author: Lakhyajit Changmai
summary: The DOM is not the source of truth. That sounds obvious, and it is the thing that breaks almost every browser agent that edits text on a page. The field fills, the save endpoint answers 200, and the value stored is empty. I hit this five times in one day on five different editors, and the fix was always the same idea: find the layer the submit handler reads from, and write to that one. Three layers, only one of which is authoritative Most text inputs on the modern web are not the node you can see. They are a stack: the DOM - what is rendered the editor document - ProseMirror state, Quill's internal model, Draft.js ContentState the application store - the React or Redux state that builds the request body element.value = ... , innerText = ... and document.execCommand(...) touch layer 1, or reach layer 2 by accident. The submit handler serialises layer 3. When nothing propagates upward, you get a clean, successful no-op. What follows is what worked on each editor. All of it was found the slow way. 1. ProseMirror: beforeinput , not execCommand ProseMirror listens for the beforeinput event and mutates its document in response to it. It does not read what you write into the DOM. const el = document . querySelector ( ' .ProseMirror ' ); el . focus (); const ev = new InputEvent ( ' beforeinput ' , { inputType : ' insertText ' , data : text , bubbles : true , cancelable : true , composed : true , }); el . dispatchEvent ( ev ); document.execCommand('insertText') and driver-level typing both produced the same result here: the text appeared in the field, Save returned success, and the stored document was one empty paragraph. 2. Tiptap: a real paste payload Tiptap is ProseMirror underneath, but its paste handler is the part you can reach. Dispatch a synthetic clipboard event carrying a real DataTransfer : const dt = new DataTransfer (); dt . setData ( ' text/plain ' , text ); const consumed = ! editorEl . dispatchEvent ( new ClipboardEvent ( ' paste ' , { clipboardData : dt , bubbles : true , cancelable : true }) ); Check consumed . dispatchEvent returns false only when a handler called preventDefault() , so that boolean is your proof the editor took the payload rather than the browser shrugging at it. 3. Quill: execCommand works, and it multiplies newlines Quill ignored the synthetic paste entirely but accepted this: editorEl . focus (); document . execCommand ( ' insertText ' , false , text ); One quirk cost me a visible edit: Quill expands paragraph breaks, so two newlines in came back as four blank lines out. Author with single newlines and re-read the result before publishing. 4. Draft.js: only trusted input, and innerText lies Draft.js (X's composer) keeps its text in its own render nodes: const stateText = composer . querySelector ( ' span[data-text="true"] ' ). textContent ; Use that as the oracle, not innerText . After an execCommand write, Draft.js leaves a sibling text node that React never reconciles, so innerText double-counts and the character counter reports a number that is not true of the state. I published a truncated post believing that counter. Synthetically, nothing works on Draft.js: beforeinput is ignored, and a synthetic paste is consumed but inserts nothing. Only a real browser-level keystroke updates its state. 5. The case that broke my own rule: editor state was also the wrong layer I was ready to end this article at write to the editor state . Then a Tiptap composer that mirrors itself into a Redux store refused to publish. I set content through the editor API and verified everything I thought mattered: the document held 1,813 characters, the update event fired, the DOM rendered the text. The request body the app sent was: { "caption" : "" , "postTitle" : "Automated text entry is a state problem, not a DOM problem" } Empty caption. The same text delivered through the clipboard paste route in section 2 reached the store, and the identical payload published at 200. Same visible result, one layer apart. Layer 2 was not authoritative either. Verify against the payload, not the page Hook the network before diagnosing anything: window . __cap = []; const open = XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open ; const send = XMLHttpRequest . prototype . send ; XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open = function ( m , u ) { this . __u = u ; this . __m = m ; return open . apply ( this , arguments ); }; XMLHttpRequest . prototype . send = function ( b ) { window . __cap . push ({ url : this . __u , method : this . __m , body : b }); return send . apply ( this , arguments ); }; Then assert exactly one of three things: the outgoing request body contains your text; the framework document contains it ( editor.state.doc.textBetween(...) , editor.getHTML() ); or a cold reload of the page shows it. The reload is the only proof that reaches layer 3. Two smaller findings that cost real time A disabled submit button is usually a validation message that moved somewhere else. In the Peerlist composer, the server's 400 string was bound to the button's disabled prop, so an over-length caption presented as a permanently dead button plus a generic error. The actual limit - 480 characters - only appeared as helper text once the content was already short enough. No counter, no warning while you are over it. On React-controlled inputs, input.value = x does nothing , because React reads through its own descriptor and overwrites you on the next render: const set = Object . getOwnPropertyDescriptor ( HTMLTextAreaElement . prototype , ' value ' ). set ; set . call ( ta , text ); ta . dispatchEvent ( new Event ( ' input ' , { bubbles : true })); ta . dispatchEvent ( new Event ( ' change ' , { bubbles : true })); The part that is not a trick Every editor in this list is behaving correctly. The bug is the assumption that what you can see is what gets saved. That assumption survives for a long time, because the failure is quiet: the UI looks right the whole way through, and the only artefacts that tell the truth are the request the app sends and the page you load ten minutes later. I build ZANCTA, a set of local-first PDF and image tools that run entirely in the browser tab, so the general shape of this problem is familiar to me: if the state you are reading is a copy of the state that matters, you will be confidently wrong.

title: Intro To Webassembly With Rust
author: Phil IPS
summary: Intro to WebAssembly with Rust Introduction WebAssembly (Wasm) is a binary instruction format for a stack-based virtual machine. It enables near-native-speed execution in web browsers and is increasingly used for performance-critical applications. Rust, with its memory safety guarantees and excellent WebAssembly support, is a perfect language for creating Wasm modules. Why Rust for WebAssembly? Rust provides: Memory safety without a garbage collector Powerful macro system for code generation Excellent tooling for WebAssembly via wasm-pack Strong community support for Wasm development Setting Up Your Environment First, install Rust if you haven't already: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1 .2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh Then install wasm-pack : cargo install wasm-pack Creating a Simple WebAssembly Module Let's create a Rust function that adds two numbers: #[no_mangle] pub extern "C" fn add ( a : i32 , b : i32 ) -> i32 { a + b } This function takes two i32 parameters and returns their sum. The #[no_mangle] attribute ensures the function name isn't mangled, and extern "C" makes it callable from JavaScript. Building the Module Compile the Rust code to WebAssembly: wasm-pack build --target web This creates a pkg directory with the Wasm file and JavaScript bindings. Using the Module in JavaScript In your HTML file: <script type= "module" > import init , { add } from ' ./pkg/your_module.js ' ; async function run () { await init (); const result = add ( 5 , 7 ); console . log ( ' 5 + 7 = ' , result ); } run (); </script> </html> Conclusion With Rust and WebAssembly, you can create high-performance web applications. This is just a simple example - explore more complex use cases like game engines, image processing, or cryptographic operations. The combination of Rust's safety and Wasm's performance opens up exciting possibilities for web development.

title: Phoenix Explained: Real-Time Web Apps That Never Stop
author: The Practical Developer
summary: Introduction Most web frameworks treat real-time features — live updates, chat, collaborative editing — as an add-on: bolt on WebSockets, manage connections yourself, hope it scales. Phoenix, released in 2015 and built on Elixir (the batch 30 post), treats real-time as the default. It inherits the Erlang VM's fault tolerance, so a crashing connection affects one user, not the server, and it adds LiveView: server-rendered pages that update live over a persistent connection, without writing JavaScript. It is the framework that made "never stops" a web feature. Channels, LiveView, and fault tolerance Phoenix's model rests on a few distinctive ideas: Channels — named topics over WebSockets, so a browser subscribes to a room, a feed, or a document, and the server pushes updates to exactly the right subscribers. LiveView — server-side rendering with live updates: user events travel to the server, the server re-renders the changed part, and only the diff travels back. Interactive pages, almost no client JavaScript. Presence — built-in tracking of who is online in a channel, so user lists and typing indicators come almost free. Fault tolerance by inheritance — every connection is an Elixir process, supervised and isolated, so failures stay small and the system heals itself (see the Elixir post for the model). A channel shows the shape — join a topic, broadcast to everyone in it: defmodule MyAppWeb . RoomChannel do use MyAppWeb , :channel def join ( "room:lobby" , _payload , socket ) do { :ok , socket } end def handle_in ( "new_msg" , %{ "body" => body }, socket ) do broadcast! ( socket , "new_msg" , %{ body: body }) { :noreply , socket } end end One process per connection, one broadcast to the whole room — and if a connection crashes, only that connection restarts. The honest trade Phoenix's trade is ecosystem and hiring: a smaller community and job market than Rails or Node, and Elixir's functional style takes adjustment. Its conventional structure is also opinionated — productive once learned, unfamiliar at first. The rule of thumb: Phoenix when real-time features and reliability matter most; Rails or Node when ecosystem depth or hiring dominates. Takeaway Phoenix is real-time web apps that never stop: channels, LiveView, and presence, on Elixir's fault-tolerant foundation. It trades mainstream ecosystem for live features that scale by default — and for apps where "live" is the product, that trade is the point. Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/phoenix-explained-real-time-web-apps.html

title: Three CSVs In, 1,272 Food Pages Out: PregNut's Boring Static Build
author: Yuriy Stasyuk
summary: PregNut is a free pregnancy food lookup I've been building since 2018. You search a food and see how 100 grams of it stacks up against the daily amounts pregnancy asks for. It has 1,272 foods and 13 nutrients, and each food gets its own page. There's no database server behind it. It's an Eleventy site that builds from three CSV files and deploys to Cloudflare Pages. I like boring stacks for side projects, and this one has stayed easy to work on through three pregnancies, so here's how it fits together. The inputs The database/ folder has three files: FoodList.csv , NutrientList.csv and daily requirements.csv . The food list has the USDA NDB number, name, food group and a warning field. The nutrient list is long and skinny, one row per food per nutrient with a value and a unit. The requirements file has the daily reference amount for each nutrient as a label like "1000 mg" or "0.3 g." All of it comes from a fixed snapshot of the USDA's SR Legacy data. USDA's final Standard Reference release was in 2018, so the numbers are frozen. For a reference site I count that as a feature. A value doesn't change under you between builds. The cost is that newer data and current product labels can differ, and the About page says that. A tiny build script instead of a dependency scripts/build-fooddata.js reads the CSVs and writes one JSON file the site uses everywhere. I wrote a minimal CSV parser for it, small enough to read in one sitting. It handles quoted fields and doubled quotes, and it strips a byte order mark if there is one. That BOM will quietly rename your first column header if you don't strip it. The requirements file has a reference list under the main table, so the parser stops when it hits the SourceId row. Reference amounts get parsed with a small regex into a number and a unit. One choice I'd make again. If the CSVs aren't present but the JSON already exists, the script prints a warning and keeps the existing JSON instead of failing. That lets a deploy work from the committed JSON alone. One page per food with pagination Eleventy's pagination does the heavy lifting. The food page template paginates over a data file with size: 1 , so every item becomes its own page. The permalink is /food/{{ food.slug }}/ , and the slug starts with the USDA number: /food/15151-shrimp-cooked/ , /food/15152-shrimp-canned/ . Food names repeat a lot in USDA data. The number keeps every URL unique without me thinking about it. The data file is also where per-page decisions live. Title overrides for pages that get search traffic, related blog posts, and special cases. The human milk record, for example, stays in the dataset but is labeled as a historical data record only and left out of the food listings. Units needed a helper. DHA is stored in grams and its benchmark is 0.3 g, while other nutrients are in mg or mcg. There's a small conversion function so comparisons always happen in the same unit. Each page shows two columns: per 100 g, and a serving based on FDA reference amounts. Cooked shrimp shows 3 oz (85 g) next to 100 g. The 100 g column is for comparing foods. The serving column is closer to what's on a plate. What the data can't do The dataset has no iodine values. Rather than fake it, the site has an iodine guide and says the data is missing. Folate is shown as DFE, which isn't the same thing as the folic acid number on a prenatal label, so that gets its own guide too. PregNut is an educational reference and isn't medical advice. Every page says so in the footer. Deploys and one contact form A GitHub Actions workflow runs npm run build and deploys with wrangler. Pushes to master go to pregnut.com. Pull requests get a preview deploy, and the link gets posted on the PR. Previews are only built for branches in the repo, and the actions are pinned to commit SHAs. The *.pages.dev hosts send X-Robots-Tag: noindex from _headers , so Google only indexes the real domain. The one dynamic piece is /api/contact , a Cloudflare Pages Function. I wanted a free email relay and picked FormSubmit, which turned out to refuse requests coming from Workers. So the function does validation, a honeypot, a timing check and rate limiting, and only then hands the browser the relay endpoint to send to. Bots that fail the checks never see it. If you want to see the output, open any food page on pregnut.com and view source. The numbers and the notes are right there in the HTML.

title: Mitigating Double Execution on External API Timeouts: A Practical Guide to Distributed Concurrency Control
author: PhenoX
summary: Mitigating Double Execution on External API Timeouts: A Practical Guide to Distributed Concurrency Control The Problem: Duplicate Execution in the Wake of Timeouts During the backend development of payment processing systems, timeout failures caused by network latency when communicating with external Payment Service Providers (PSPs) are a notorious source of data inconsistencies. Analyzing transaction logs reveals a recurring post-timeout race condition: A client initiates a payment request to the API server. The API server dispatches an outbound HTTP request to the external PSP. The external PSP successfully executes the transaction on their ledger. However, due to a transient network severance or packet drop during response transmission, the API server triggers a gateway timeout (such as 504 Gateway Timeout or socket read timeout). The client application (or an upstream resilient retry mechanism like an exponential backoff worker) interprets this as an unhandled failure and promptly dispatches an identical retry request with the exact same parameters. While the first request is still in-flight or already completed in the background, the server receives the retry and spawns a secondary thread/process to process the payment once again. To prevent duplicate charges, it is not enough to simply reject identical transactions after the fact. The architecture demands an atomic, in-flight state detection mechanism that immediately intercepts and throttles concurrent or duplicated incoming requests . Architectural Sequence & Design Principles To safeguard against duplicate execution across distributed nodes, our design focuses on two critical pillars: Strict Request Identity (Idempotency Key) : Rather than relying solely on a client-supplied transaction_id , we compute a cryptographic SHA-256 digest of the normalized request payload and concatenate it with the transaction identifier. This prevents tampering, payload mismatch, or unintentional reuse across divergent mutations. Two-Tier Concurrency Control : We implement an in-memory, high-throughput distributed lock powered by Redis ( SETNX with a bounded TTL) to absorb incoming spikes and shed redundant retries at the edge. This is backed by a permanent persistence layer (RDB) equipped with a database-level UNIQUE constraint to serve as the ultimate ledger integrity barrier. sequenceDiagram autonumber actor Client as "Client Application" participant API as "API Gateway / Server" participant Redis as "Redis (Distributed Mutex)" participant PSP as "External PSP API" Client->>API: "Submit Payment Request (Payload)" API->>API: "1. Ultra-fast Deserialization & Pydantic Validation" API->>API: "2. Generate Idempotency Key (TXN ID + SHA-256 Digest)" API->>Redis: "3. acquire_lock (SETNX with TTL)" alt "Lock Acquired (Initial Request)" Redis-->>API: "Success (Lock Granted)" API->>PSP: "Outbound HTTP API Call" PSP-->>API: "200 OK (Payment Processed)" API->>Redis: "4. release_lock (Optional cleanup or state update)" API-->>Client: "200 OK (Payment Success)" else "Lock Conflict (Duplicate / Concurrent Retry)" Redis-->>API: "Conflict (Key Already Present)" API-->>Client: "409 Conflict (Duplicate Request Detected)" end Production-Ready Verification Code The following Python script demonstrates an end-to-end idempotency validation flow. It integrates high-speed JSON serialization ( orjson with fallback to standard json ), strict schema validation via Pydantic v2, and an in-memory idempotency coordinator modeling Redis atomic semantics ( SETNX with TTL expiration). try : import orjson HAS_ORJSON = True except ImportError : import json HAS_ORJSON = False import hashlib import time from typing import Optional from pydantic import BaseModel , Field , field_validator def serialize_json ( data : dict , indent : bool = False ) -> bytes : """ Serializes a dictionary using orjson if available, falling back to standard json. """ if HAS_ORJSON : option = orjson . OPT_SORT_KEYS | ( orjson . OPT_INDENT_2 if indent else 0 ) return orjson . dumps ( data , option = option ) else : indent_val = 2 if indent else None return json . dumps ( data , sort_keys = True , indent = indent_val ). encode ( " utf-8 " ) def deserialize_json ( data : bytes ) -> dict : """ Deserializes raw JSON bytes using orjson if available, falling back to standard json. """ if HAS_ORJSON : return orjson . loads ( data ) else : return json . loads ( data . decode ( " utf-8 " )) class PaymentRequest ( BaseModel ): transaction_id : str = Field (..., description = " Unique client-side transaction identifier " ) amount : int = Field (..., gt = 0 , description = " Transaction amount in minor units or base integer " ) currency : str = Field (..., min_length = 3 , max_length = 3 , description = " ISO-4217 3-letter currency code " ) @field_validator ( " currency " ) @classmethod def case_upper ( cls , v : str ) -> str : return v . upper () class IdempotencyManager : """ Simulates distributed mutual exclusion using Redis atomic primitives (SETNX + TTL). """ def __init__ ( self ): # In a real-world production setup, inject a redis.Redis or redis.asyncio client instance. self . _redis_store : dict [ str , float ] = {} def generate_idempotency_key ( self , req : PaymentRequest ) -> str : # Deterministically serialize the payload and compute its SHA-256 digest serialized = serialize_json ( req . model_dump ()) body_hash = hashlib . sha256 ( serialized ). hexdigest () return f " idempotency: { req . transaction_id } : { body_hash } " def acquire_lock ( self , key : str , ttl_seconds : int = 30 ) -> bool : """ Emulates Redis atomic SET key value NX EX ttl_seconds operation. """ current_time = time . time () # Evict expired keys (simulating Redis active/passive TTL eviction) if key in self . _redis_store : if self . _redis_store [ key ] < current_time : del self . _redis_store [ key ] else : # Lock is active: treat as concurrent duplicate or re-entrant request return False # Acquire lock and set lease expiration timestamp self . _redis_store [ key ] = current_time + ttl_seconds return True def release_lock ( self , key : str ) -> None : """ Releases the lock on transaction completion or failure. """ if key in self . _redis_store : del self . _redis_store [ key ] def process_external_payment ( request_json : bytes ) -> dict : """ Entry point for external payment orchestration with end-to-end idempotency protection. """ # 1. High-throughput deserialization try : raw_data = deserialize_json ( request_json ) except Exception as e : return { " status " : " error " , " message " : f " Invalid JSON payload: { e } " } # 2. Strict domain model validation via Pydantic v2 try : payment_req = PaymentRequest ( ** raw_data ) except Exception as e : return { " status " : " error " , " message " : f " Validation error: { e } " } manager = IdempotencyManager () idempotency_key = manager . generate_idempotency_key ( payment_req ) # 3. Distributed atomic lock acquisition check if not manager . acquire_lock ( idempotency_key , ttl_seconds = 10 ): # Detect and shed uncoordinated retries or concurrent duplicates return { " status " : " conflict " , " message " : " Duplicate request detected. Transaction is already in progress or completed. " } try : # 4. Secondary defense: Insert transaction record into relational database # with a UNIQUE index constraint on (transaction_id, body_hash). # Simulating external PSP gateway network round-trip and potential delay time . sleep ( 0.1 ) response_data = { " status " : " success " , " transaction_id " : payment_req . transaction_id , " amount " : payment_req . amount , " currency " : payment_req . currency , " processed_at " : time . time () } return response_data finally : # Release transient execution lock (or adjust retention policy according to business requirements) manager . release_lock ( idempotency_key ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : # Construct a sample payment payload payload = serialize_json ({ " transaction_id " : " TXN-202X-9999 " , " amount " : 5000 , " currency " : " jpy " }) print ( " --- Initial Request Execution --- " ) res1 = process_external_payment ( payload ) print ( serialize_json ( res1 , indent = True ). decode ( " utf-8 " )) print ( " \n --- Duplicate Request Simulation (Immediate Retry on Assumed Timeout) --- " ) res2 = process_external_payment ( payload ) print ( serialize_json ( res2 , indent = True ). decode ( " utf-8 " )) 💡 For immediate deployment: The complete source code suite (ZIP) for this architecture is available on Gumroad for $0+ (Pay What You Want). Production Insights & Operational Best Practices 1. TTL (Time-To-Live) Calibration Setting an optimal lease duration for your distributed locks requires balancing two opposing risks: TTL is too short : If an upstream PSP experiences an extended processing delay and the lock expires while the thread is still awaiting a response, a concurrent retry will acquire a new lock, leading directly to duplicate charges. TTL is too long : If the processing application node crashes ungracefully before releasing the mutex, subsequent valid client retries remain locked out in a deadlocked state until the TTL elapses. In practice, the TTL should be calculated as: $$\text{Lock TTL} = \text{External HTTP Client Timeout} + \text{Clock Drift Margin} + \text{Grace Period}$$ For payment integrations where downstream PSP read timeouts are configured to 15 seconds, a distributed lock TTL between 20 to 30 seconds is generally standard. 2. Dual-Layer Defense: Redis Mutex + RDBMS Unique Constraints Redis serves as an in-memory, low-latency filter to absorb fast-frequency retry storms before they saturate database connection pools. However, distributed in-memory systems face failovers, asynchronous replication lag, and potential data loss during cluster topology shifts. Therefore, absolute consistency demands that the durable storage layer (such as PostgreSQL or MySQL) enforces a strict UNIQUE index constraint on (transaction_id) or (idempotency_key) .
