title: Catchment: answering five questions about a place with one database
author: Harish Kotra (he/him)
summary: "Can I rent here?" is not a question. It is five questions wearing a trench coat. Which ward is this? Which zone? How far is the nearest lake? Is there a hospital close enough? Is there a school close enough? In Hyderabad you answer that today by opening a municipal PDF, a ward map, a maps app for distances, and then making a decision on vibes anyway. Catchment answers the whole stack from a single shape. Tap a point or draw an area, and it comes back with a verdict plus the real metres behind every rule. Then it reverses the question: give it your rules once and it searches the entire city for every place that passes. This is the technical story of building it, including the four things that behaved differently from how I assumed, because those are the parts worth writing down. Why a spatial database and not a spreadsheet The naive version of this app is a JSON file with polygons and a loop. It works for 145 wards. It falls apart the moment you ask "what is within 500 metres of this point" for 2,566 places, because you have turned a query into a computation the browser has to survive. The whole argument for Catchment is that the distance, the containment and the threshold comparison are questions a database should answer. So the profile of the project is deliberately shaped around the least used corner of Appwrite TablesDB: polygon and point columns, spatial indexes, and the intersects and distanceLessThan operators. That decision has a cost. It means the app cannot lie about where its numbers come from, because the query that produced them is part of the answer. That turned out to be the best feature in the product. The data Real boundaries, real places, rebuilt from source: 145 wards, 5 zones, and the city boundary from DataMeet , Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation, derived from OpenStreetMap 320 water bodies and 2,566 places (hospitals, clinics, schools, colleges, stations) from OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API 1,624 candidate cells generated as a grid over the city, each measured against water, hospitals, schools and transit at build time Basemap from OpenFreeMap, geocoding from Nominatim, both keyless npm run fixtures re-fetches all of it, repairs multipart geometry, simplifies rings and rebuilds the grid. The raw API responses are committed so a clone can rebuild offline. The schema Seven tables, twelve indexes, five of them spatial. Table Rows Geometry Indexes wards 145 boundary polygon, center point boundary_spatial , name_key zones 5 boundary polygon boundary_spatial water 320 boundary polygon (hull), center point, polys_json boundary_spatial , center_spatial pois 2,566 location point, kind location_spatial , kind_key cells 1,624 location point plus four distances location_spatial and one key index per distance checks grows location point, ruleset, verdict none meta 1 source and bounding box none The load bearing decision is in water . The exact geometry of every lake lives in polys_json , and the boundary column holds a convex hull of all parts. That split exists because of the first bug below. The three queries that make it work One: which ward contains this shape. Polygons are queried by intersection, and a drawn area can touch several wards at once, which is the correct answer rather than an edge case. const rows = await this . rows ( " wards " , [ Query . intersects ( " boundary " , ring ), Query . select ([ " name " , " number " , " zone " , " area_km2 " ]), ]); Two: how far is the nearest water. This one had to be asked twice, for reasons covered below. const ring = bufferRing ( point , metres ); const [ touching , centred ] = await Promise . all ([ this . rows ( " water " , [ Query . intersects ( " boundary " , ring ), select ]), this . rows ( " water " , [ Query . distanceLessThan ( " center " , point , metres ), select ]), ]); const merged = new Map < string , Water > (); for ( const row of [... touching , ... centred ]) merged . set ( String ( row . $id ), toWater ( row )); const inRange = [... merged . values ()]. filter (( w ) => distToPolysM ( point , w . polys ) <= metres ); The database narrows the candidates. The metre figure on screen is then computed from the geometry that came back with the row. That division of labour is the whole design: index for speed, geometry for truth. Three: the reverse query. Each cell stores the four distances it was measured against, so the city wide search is an ordinary indexed comparison instead of 1,624 geometry tests at request time. const rows = await this . rows ( " cells " , [ Query . greaterThanEqual ( " water_m " , rules . waterMinM ), Query . lessThanEqual ( " hospital_m " , rules . hospitalMaxM ), Query . lessThanEqual ( " school_m " , rules . schoolMaxM ), Query . greaterThanEqual ( " station_m " , rules . transitMaxM ), ]); With the default "live somewhere" rules, 546 of 1,624 places pass. That number is in the tests, so if a refactor quietly changes it, the suite says so. Four things that did not behave as expected 1. A lake with four parts is not a lake with one part Hussain Sagar is one of the largest lakes in the city, 3.55 km². Its OpenStreetMap geometry is a relation with four polygon parts. The loader stored polys[0][0] , the first ring of the first part, which is a 27 point sliver. The insert succeeded, the row count was right, the index reported available , and every spatial query near the lake returned nothing. The app did the worst possible thing: it looked fine. The fix is a convex hull over every part for the search column, while the exact geometry stays in polys_json for measurement. A hull is a superset, so the index can over return but never miss, and the metre figure is still exact. const searchRing = ( polys : number [][][][]) => { const points : number [][] = []; for ( const part of polys ) for ( const point of part [ 0 ]) points . push ( point ); return convexHull ( points ); }; Osman Sagar's stored ring went from about 200 points to 16, and the queries started answering. 2. Distance operators are for points Query.distanceLessThan("boundary", point, metres) on a polygon column does not throw. It returns zero rows. That is worth reading twice, because if your code has a fallback that quietly computes locally when the database returns nothing, your app will be correct on your machine and subtly wrong for everyone else, and no test will notice unless you write one that can. The right answer is to ask the polygon column something it can answer, which is intersection, and to complement it with a centre distance query on a second spatial index. 3. Intersection is boundary based, not containment The complement query exists because of this: a query polygon is treated as an outline. A pond that sits entirely inside your 500 metre circle never touches the circle's edge, so intersects alone does not return it. Ask both questions, union the results, then measure exactly. There is a test for precisely this, and it is small enough to be unambiguous: a 0.026 km² pond called Erra Kunta, a test point 250 metres east of it, and a 500 metre search radius. The intersection returns nothing. The centre query returns the pond at 157 metres. The app gets the union. 4. Small schema details that reject big features Two Appwrite constraints cost time and are worth knowing before you start: A spatial index cannot be built on a nullable column. If your geometry columns are optional, index creation fails with column_index_invalid , and the fix is to mark the column required and repopulate. The bulk rows endpoint takes row objects, not { rowId, data } wrappers. My first loader wrote the wrapper, and the API answered "Missing required attribute name" because it saw no attributes at all. The setup script now probes which row shape the server accepts and keeps the one that works. There is also a cloud level trap: an Appwrite Cloud project is pinned to one region, and the wrong endpoint answers 401 Project is not accessible in this region . npm run detect:region probes every region with the project ID and saves the one that answers, which turns a confusing auth error into one command. Design constraints, not decoration The brief was that a 70 year old and a 17 year old should both be able to use this without being taught. That became engineering constraints: 17px base type with three text sizes, so enlarging does not break the layout 46 to 56px targets, with a hard 44px minimum enforced by scripts/audit.mjs at five viewport widths AA contrast, measured rather than eyeballed No icon only buttons, no long press, no hidden gesture: every action is a word Pass and fail stated in text, never colour alone A first visit hint that disappears on first use The verdict card scrolls itself into view on a phone, because a result below the fold is a result nobody sees Accessibility regressions are build failures here, not polish. That is the only way they survive contact with a deadline. Making the database visible Every verdict carries a receipt. Under each result there is a Show control that lists the table, the operator and the milliseconds behind that number. It is not a debug mode. It is the argument of the product: the distance is real, the boundary is real, and here is the query that produced it. That choice also made the project testable in a way that is hard to fake. npm run verify:appwrite runs 13 checks against the live project, each printing a timing, and exits non zero when anything fails: pass spatial: water bodies near Hussain Sagar (118 ms) 1 rows · nearest Hussain Sagar at 0 m (3.55 km²) pass spatial: a pond entirely inside the searched circle (357 ms) Erra Kunta at 157 m pass spatial: hospitals and clinics within 2 km of Charminar (185 ms) 43 rows pass thresholds: cells at least 300 m from water and within 1 km of a hospital (256 ms) 1031 of 1624 cells pass spatial: wards overlapping a drawn ring (116 ms) 6 rows · Ward 91 Khairatabad, Ward 88 Bholakpur Those lines are the demo. Not because they prove the app works, but because they show what kind of app it is. What I would build next The honest next steps, in order of how much they would teach: Saved rulesets with row permissions. Let people keep "our rules" as a row that belongs to them, not to a server key. That is the natural place to use per user permissions properly. A public audit endpoint. Given the inputs of a shared verdict, recompute it. A result you can hand to someone and have them check is worth more than a screenshot. Offline sync. The last verdict and the rules surviving a train tunnel is a real use case for someone checking a place on site. More rule dimensions. Flood extent, noise, metro proximity. The engine is a list of measurements, so the hard part is data, not code. VectorsDB over place descriptions to answer "somewhere like this neighbourhood", which is the question that follows "which places pass" once people start using it. Run it git clone https://github.com/harishkotra/catchment.git cd catchment npm install npm run dev No keys needed. Add Appwrite credentials and the header switches from Local cache to Appwrite TablesDB , and the same queries run against the live database. The code is MIT licensed, the data is ODbL, and the parts that took the longest to learn are the parts documented in the README. If you are building anything spatial on TablesDB, start from the four gotchas above and save yourself an evening. Code & more: https://www.dailybuild.xyz/project/296-catchment

title: The Agentic Development Lifecycle - The Four Pillars
author: Praveen Govindaraj
summary: Your context window is a budget, not a bucket - Chapter 6 · Why giving your agent more context can make it worse Why giving your AI coding agent more context can make it perform worse When an AI coding agent gets stuck, the instinct is usually to give it more context. More files. More documentation. More conversation history. A longer CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. Maybe the entire repository. The assumption is simple: if the agent knows more, it should make better decisions. But experiments suggest otherwise. In one SWE-agent experiment, showing the agent a relevant file in a 100-line window produced an 18.0% success rate. Showing the entire file dropped that to 12.7%. The agent had more information. Its performance got worse. This is one of the most important lessons in building reliable AI coding workflows: Your context window is a budget, not a bucket. The goal isn't to give an agent as much information as possible. It's to give it the right information at the right time. More context doesn't automatically mean better results Consider how you debug an unfamiliar codebase. You probably don't read every source file before fixing a bug. You start with the error, identify the relevant module, inspect its dependencies, and follow the evidence. You narrow the problem before expanding your investigation. AI agents need a similar discipline. Every model call receives a context payload: the instructions, relevant code, conversation history, tool results, and other information available for that decision. The size of the context window tells you how much information the model can receive. It doesn't tell you how much information it can use effectively. In the SWE-agent experiment, the results looked like this: Showing too little information can hurt performance. But showing everything can hurt, too. This is not an argument for always using shorter prompts. It's an argument for being deliberate about what goes into them. Context has two failure modes When an agent performs poorly, context problems generally fall into two broad categories. Context starvation The agent doesn't have enough information to complete the task. For example: • It edits a function without seeing its callers. • It changes an API without seeing the expected response format. • It modifies a test without understanding the production behavior. • It follows a coding convention that the repository no longer uses. The solution is to provide the missing information. Context dilution The agent has the necessary information, but it is surrounded by so much unrelated material that the relevant details become harder to use. For example: • A simple bug fix comes with the entire conversation history. • A small refactor includes documentation for unrelated modules. • A coding task begins with thousands of tokens of general instructions. • Tool output overwhelms the actual error or result the agent needs to inspect. The solution is to remove noise and make relevant information easier to find. These problems need opposite remedies. Adding more context may fix starvation while making dilution worse. A practical diagnostic When an agent produces a poor result, try a simple experiment: Reduce the context payload by roughly half and rerun the task. • If performance improves or stays about the same, the original context may have contained unnecessary information. • If performance gets worse, the removed information may have been important. This isn't a universal benchmark or a substitute for controlled evaluation. It's a useful debugging technique for understanding whether your agent needs more information or better information selection. Bigger context windows don't eliminate the problem Model context windows have grown significantly. That makes it possible to include more code, documentation, tool output, and history in a single request. But greater capacity doesn't guarantee that every additional token is useful. Research into long-context behavior has documented limitations commonly described as the lost-in-the-middle effect: information can be harder to use when it appears in certain positions within a long input. Chroma's Context Rot study examined 18 models and reported declining reliability as input length increased across several tasks. The study is useful evidence of the problem, although it comes from a company that sells vector database technology and should be considered alongside other evidence. The practical takeaway is straightforward: A model's maximum context length is a capacity limit, not a recommended prompt size. Think of it like memory in a software system. Having more available memory doesn't mean every object should remain in memory forever. Good systems still manage what they load, retain, cache, and discard. The same principle applies to AI agents. Four ways to manage context If context is a budget, how should we spend it? There are four useful techniques. A. Compact the context Long-running agents accumulate information: • Previous decisions • Intermediate reasoning summaries • Tool results • Failed attempts • Old instructions • Repeated descriptions of the task Some of that information is valuable. Some is no longer relevant. Compaction means preserving the important state while removing unnecessary detail. For example, instead of retaining a long debugging conversation, keep a concise summary: Task: Fix incorrect pagination in the customer API. Findings: The database query returns the correct number of rows. The bug is in the page-offset calculation. Existing tests cover page 1 but not page 2. Files: src/api/customers.ts tests/customers.test.ts Next step: Add a regression test for page 2, then correct the offset calculation. This gives the next model call a useful starting point without carrying every previous interaction forward. The key is to preserve facts, decisions, constraints, and next steps—not every detail of the journey. B. Offload large tool outputs Tools can return far more information than an agent needs. A repository search might return hundreds of matches. A test command might produce thousands of lines. A log file might contain one useful error buried in repetitive output. Instead of inserting everything into the model's context, keep the full output outside the conversation and expose a smaller, relevant result. For example: Test suite: 248 tests Passed: 247 Failed: 1 Failing test: tests/customers.test.ts::pagination_returns_second_page Relevant error: Expected customer ID 21, received customer ID 1. If the agent needs more detail, it can fetch the relevant section. This is the principle behind tool-output offloading: store the full result, but bring only the necessary portion into context. C. Use progressive disclosure Don't load every instruction, document, or tool description at the beginning of every task. Start with a small amount of general guidance. Let the agent discover more specific information when the task requires it. For example, a repository might contain: AGENTS.md docs/ architecture.md testing.md deployment.md database.md The root AGENTS.md can explain the project's structure and point the agent toward specialized documents. A database task can load database.md. A deployment task can load deployment.md. This keeps the initial context focused while making deeper information available on demand. The distinction matters: good context engineering doesn't mean hiding information forever. It means avoiding unnecessary information before it becomes relevant. D. Reset the context when the task changes Long-running conversations can accumulate outdated assumptions, completed work, failed experiments, and irrelevant details. Sometimes summarizing the existing conversation isn't enough. Starting a fresh model call with a concise handoff is cleaner. Think of an engineer handing work to a teammate at the end of a shift. The handoff should include: • What has been completed • What remains unresolved • Which files have changed • What has been tested • Which decisions must not be revisited • What the next step should be The new agent doesn't need the entire history. It needs the current state of the work. Reset the conversation, not the project's knowledge. Keep durable information in files, tests, issue descriptions, and other artifacts that survive the context reset. Your AGENTS.md can become a source of noise Repository-level context files are now common in AI-assisted development. Files such as AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and copilot-instructions.md can help agents understand a codebase without repeatedly rediscovering its conventions. But they can also accumulate stale or redundant guidance. A useful instruction file might explain: • How to run tests • Where important modules live • Which conventions are mandatory • What generated files must not be edited • Where to find specialized instructions An unhelpful one might include pages of generic advice, duplicate documentation, outdated commands, and rules that contradict the codebase. The problem gets worse when agents maintain these files by rewriting them wholesale. Repeated regeneration can gradually erase specific details, simplify important exceptions, or replace concrete instructions with generic summaries. A safer approach is incremental maintenance: Read the existing file. Identify the specific information that has changed. Update only the relevant section. Preserve useful details and exceptions. Remove instructions only when they are demonstrably obsolete or redundant. Edit context files. Don't casually regenerate them. Treat them like maintained source code, not disposable prompt text. Context engineering has a limit Better context selection is important, but it isn't the entire solution to reliable AI development. Eventually, an agent needs more than instructions about the codebase. It needs a system that helps it act correctly and verify its work. That means thinking about three related areas: • Context engineering: What information should the agent receive? • Harness engineering: What tools, constraints, and feedback loops govern its actions? • Environment and repository structure: How can the system make correct actions easier and mistakes easier to detect? A carefully written AGENTS.md cannot compensate for missing tests. A larger context window cannot make an unreliable tool reliable. A detailed instruction cannot guarantee that a change works. Context helps the agent make decisions. The surrounding development system helps those decisions become dependable results. That is where the next stage of agentic development begins. Try this in your repository Pick a coding agent you use regularly and inspect its main context file—perhaps AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md. Try this small experiment: Make a copy of the file. Remove roughly one-third of the instructions that are generic, duplicated, outdated, or irrelevant to most tasks. Keep essential constraints, commands, architecture notes, and project-specific conventions. Run the same representative coding task with the original and reduced versions. Compare the resulting code, test outcomes, and unnecessary tool calls. Don't optimize for the shortest possible file. Optimize for the most useful instructions per token. If performance drops, investigate what important information was removed. If performance stays the same or improves, you've found context that may not have been earning its place. The takeaway A bigger context window gives your agent more room. It doesn't automatically give the agent better judgment. Reliable agentic development requires deliberate choices about what enters the context, what stays outside it, what gets retrieved on demand, and when the agent should start fresh. Don't ask how much context your agent can hold. Ask which information deserves to be there. How long is your CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md today—and when was the last time a human actually edited it? This post is based on Chapter 6 of The Agentic Development Lifecycle. Read the full chapter: Context Engineering — The Budget, Not the Bucket

title: Do AI agent skills actually improve results? How I test them, including the ones that failed
author: Tim Schroeder
summary: A skill file (a SKILL.md with instructions an agent loads on demand) can easily make an agent's answer look more thorough. Whether it makes the answer more correct is a separate question, and you cannot answer it by reading a few outputs. I publish ten skills, and before any of them goes out I want a number that says it beat the plain model on tasks the skill was never tuned for. I had Claude Code build the evaluation harness and run the evaluations under my rules. This post covers how the harness works and what it found, including the skills that did not help. Why "it feels better" isn't evidence Our first evals were written by each skill's author. They were regex checks for the issues the skill was supposed to catch. On those, MCP Mechanic went from 0.956 to 1.000 and Blueprint Probe from 0.889 to 1.000 (9 runs per condition). Both looked like clear wins. The script's own method note explains the catch: the checks "test whether named issues and safe behaviours appear, not overall answer quality." An author who knows what the skill says can write tasks that reward the skill's vocabulary. When a separate evaluator tested Blueprint Probe on new tasks, it found no gain at all in what mattered most: finding the flaws. The rule I approved, recorded in our decisions log: a new original skill publishes only after lint, a security scan, an author eval, and a blind independent eval where it beats the baseline. Any change to the skill between rounds is disclosed, and a round that reuses earlier tasks is labelled weaker evidence. The setup The independent harness is one TypeScript script ( eval-independent.ts ). This is what it does. Piece What it does Tasks Written by a separate evaluator agent from the skill's public description only ( skill.json and README), without reading SKILL.md Freeze Tasks, fixtures, rubrics and answer keys are hashed into FREEZE.txt before the first run; every run aborts on a hash mismatch Conditions Baseline (no skill) vs skill (the skill folder copied into .claude/skills/ , minus its evals/ ) Prompt Identical in both conditions, and it never names the skill Isolation Fresh temp dir per run, headless claude -p , file tools only, no MCP servers, deny rules on the home tree Scoring Deterministic checks on the answer or the files the agent left behind, plus a blind rubric score from a separate grader model Combined 0.5 × share of hard checks passed + 0.5 × mean rubric score The freeze check is three lines. If someone edits a task after freezing, the run refuses to start: const hash = frozenHash ( slug ); const freezeTxt = fs . readFileSync ( path . join ( evalDir ( slug ), " FREEZE.txt " ), " utf8 " ); if ( ! freezeTxt . includes ( hash )) throw new Error ( `Frozen hash mismatch: computed ${ hash } , not in FREEZE.txt. Tasks changed after freezing.` ); The only difference between conditions is one copy, and that copy skips the skill's own tests: if ( cond === " skill " ) fs . cpSync ( path . join ( REPO , " skills " , slug ), skillDest , { recursive : true , filter : ( src ) => ! src . split ( path . sep ). includes ( " evals " ) }); The grader (Opus) gets one answer at a time, in a seeded shuffled order, under a hashed blind ID. Before the answer reaches it, the skill's name, its install path and even the word "skill" are scrubbed: function redact ( s : string ) { for ( const n of redactNames ) s = s . replace ( new RegExp ( n , " gi " ), " [redacted] " ); return s . replace ( / \. claude \/ skills \/[^\s )`'" ] */g , " [redacted-path] " ). replace ( / \b skills ?\b /gi , " [redacted] " ); } The grader runs with no tools. In the generic mode it scores each rubric item 0, 0.5 or 1, and it lists any claim in the answer it believes is factually wrong. That false_claims list turned out to matter more than the score. What we found Wins Skill Baseline With skill Runs per condition MCP Mechanic (first round) 0.876 0.976 15 First Reply 1.2.0 0.735 1.000 12 Cost Compass 1.0.2 0.766 0.943 12 Prompt Proof 1.0.2 0.788 0.944 12 These are combined check-plus-rubric scores, not percentages of improvement. Prompt Proof's row hides a problem, covered below. The clearest single result came from MCP Mechanic. One task had the user paste a database password and ask for a server to be added. All three baseline runs repeated the password in an export command, and one of them also deleted the existing server from .mcp.json . Across the five tasks, 3 of 15 baseline runs leaked a secret, against 0 of 15 with the skill. All hard file checks passed in 12 of 15 baseline runs and in 15 of 15 skill runs. The skill runs were not slip-free, though: the grader flagged claims in 6 of 15 of them against 1 of 15 baseline runs. Two of those flags were the grader's own mistake (see below), and in 2 runs the answer said "two syntax errors" while fixing three. Skills also cost something. MCP Mechanic runs averaged 19 s and $0.054 (the CLI's reported cost) against 13 s and $0.034 without the skill. No gain: Blueprint Probe Blueprint Probe reviews automation designs. Three blueprints carried 17 planted flaws, and a fourth blueprint was clean. Planted-flaw recall was 1.00 in both conditions . The base model found every flaw without help. The skill did deliver its promised format. It produced a findings table with blocker/major/minor ratings in 12 of 12 runs, against 0 of 12 for baseline. It never called anything in the clean design a blocker. But it still rated 2 to 4 operational nits as "major" in every clean-design run, 9 majors in all, and the grader judged that none of them needed to be major. The verdict on record is "verified with limits": this test does not show that it finds more problems than the model alone. Worse than baseline: Guide Proof 1.0.0 Guide Proof checks whether a setup guide can be followed. Version 1.0.0 scored 0.857 against a baseline of 0.888 . In other words, installing it made results worse. The per-run records show why: On a GitHub Actions deploy guide, it missed the host and username secrets as prerequisites in all 3 runs. On a guide written to be clean, it failed the "gives a positive verdict" check in all 3 runs. The grader flagged claims such as a guide "never mentions creating a project" when Part 1 says "create a project", and wrong step and line numbers. Version 1.1.0 told the model to quote step labels instead of computing numbers, to search before saying something is missing, and to count CI secrets as needs. It then scored 0.871 → 0.933, with false-claim runs at 5 → 1. That round reused the same frozen tasks that showed the problem, so it is weaker evidence. Even then, 1.1.0 was still below baseline on one of the four tasks (0.917 vs 1.000), more than the 0.05 margin our marketplace standard allows. It was not shortlisted for marketplaces: the first round lost to baseline and the second reused its tasks, so the evidence is weak. A high score hiding a defect: First Reply 1.1.1 First Reply drafts the first SMS and email to a real estate lead. Version 1.1.1 scored 0.990 against 0.713, which looked excellent. Then the false-claim lists showed a pattern. In 6 of the 12 skill runs, the grader flagged a wrong character count or word count, for example "Email subject is stated as 52 characters; it is actually 42." The skill had told the model to state the SMS length, and the model is not reliable at counting characters. Version 1.2.0 removed that instruction. On the same frozen tasks it scored 1.000 against 0.735, with false-claim runs at 2 against 4 for baseline. Held, then fixed: Prompt Proof 1.0.2 Prompt Proof 1.0.2 beat baseline on score (0.944 vs 0.788) but had grader-flagged false claims in 8 of 12 runs against 4 of 12 for baseline. Under the distribution standard, a false-claim pattern that the skill causes must be fixed before packaging, so it was held. Version 1.1.0 added rules to quote prompt text exactly and to report nothing as present that cannot be quoted. On the same frozen tasks it reached 0.952 vs 0.820, with false-claim runs at 2 of 12 against 4 of 12. 1.1.0 was then released on GitHub and the site, and the record notes that the re-run used the same frozen tasks. It now meets our marketplace evaluation bar but has not been packaged for a marketplace. One skill is still unresolved. Context Trim 1.1.0 scored 0.942 → 0.989, but its false-claim runs went up , from 6 to 10. The next version adds rules, but it has not been re-evaluated, and its page says so. The grader is wrong sometimes too In the MCP Mechanic round, the grader marked two skill answers down for a "false claim" about how Claude Code treats an unset ${VAR} in an MCP config. The evaluation record checked the Claude Code MCP docs on 2026-10-21 and found that the skill was right and the grader was wrong. The corrections are recorded next to the results (the rubric would rise from 0.952 to 0.967) but are not applied to the published aggregates. The grader's own counts are approximate too: some of its First Reply flags say "about 232". The harness had a bug of its own as well. Under --permission-mode acceptEdits , headless Claude Code refused to write .mcp.json , because that is a protected config file. That would have failed every MCP task for reasons unrelated to the skill. The first attempt was stopped and archived. The scored runs used bypassPermissions with explicit deny rules, and the reason is documented in the script. How to read small samples These numbers are directional at best: Repeats. The first rounds used 3 repeats per task and condition, and later rounds used 2. A per-task comparison is therefore 3 runs against 3, or 2 against 2. Same-vendor grader. A Claude model graded a Claude model, and it made the errors described above. Synthetic fixtures. The inputs were written for the test (First Reply's leads and listings are fictional), and no MCP server was actually started. Ceiling effects. When baseline recall is already 1.00, or the skill scores 1.000, the test cannot show any further difference. Explicit prompts. In the first round the skill fired in 15 of 15 (MCP Mechanic) and 12 of 12 (Blueprint Probe) runs, but the prompts clearly asked for the task. Whether it fires on vaguer requests is untested. Firing is not guaranteed either: in the Cost Compass round in the table, the skill fired in 10 of 12 skill runs. Reused tasks. A fix validated on the tasks that revealed the bug can overfit to them. Leaks happen. In one batch, a task writer listed skill folders after finishing its tasks and saw two author-eval file names that resembled two of its own tasks. It opened no skill file, the tasks were frozen as written, and the incident is recorded. The practical habit: read the per-task scores and the false-claim lists, not just the mean. A minimal recipe you can copy 1. Write tasks from the promise, not the instructions. Here is a real task from First Reply's frozen set, trimmed: { "id" : "F2-renter-pets" , "fixture" : "fixtures/F2" , "prompt" : "Rental inquiry from RentNest in rental-inquiry.txt. My info is in agent.md. Can you draft the first reply, text and email?" , "checks" : [ { "id" : "C-optout" , "kind" : "must_match" , "pattern" : "reply STOP|text STOP|STOP to (opt[- ]?out|unsubscribe|end|stop|cancel)" }, { "id" : "C-not-claimed-sent" , "kind" : "must_not_match" , "pattern" : "(?<!(nothing|not|never|n't) ) \\ b(I've|I have|has been|have been|was|were) (successfully |now |already )?sent \\ b" } ], "rubric" : [ { "id" : "R2" , "text" : "Does not state the pet policy, pet fees, breed or weight limits, or that the unit is available by March 1; says the agent will confirm the pet policy instead." } ], "answerKey" : { "mustNotDo" : [ "Say pets are or are not allowed" , "Quote pet deposit/fee" , "Confirm March 1 availability" ] } } Include at least one trap or clean case. A skill that finds problems should be tested on input that has none. 2. Freeze with a hash. The harness hashes a sorted manifest of per-file SHA-256 lines. This shell one-liner reproduces the hash in First Reply's FREEZE.txt (checked for this article): cd frozen && find . -type f -print0 | LC_ALL = C sort -z | xargs -0 shasum -a 256 | shasum -a 256 Check the hash before every run, and refuse to re-freeze. 3. Run two conditions with everything else equal. These are the flags our harness passes for each run (taken from the script; not re-run for this article): const args = [ " -p " , task . prompt , " --model " , AGENT_MODEL , " --output-format " , " stream-json " , " --verbose " , " --tools " , tf . agentTools , " --setting-sources " , " project " , " --strict-mcp-config " , " --mcp-config " , ' {"mcpServers":{}} ' , " --no-session-persistence " , " --permission-mode " , " bypassPermissions " , " --settings " , JSON . stringify ( DENY )]; Log from the stream whether the skill was actually invoked. A "skill" run in which the skill never fired is just a second baseline. 4. Score checks deterministically. This is the core of the generic check mode: const hit = new RegExp ( c . pattern , " i " ). test ( text ); return { id : c . id , pass : c . kind === " must_not_match " ? ! hit : hit , soft : !! c . soft }; 5. Grade blind, and ask for false claims. The grader prompt has this shape, trimmed: You are grading one answer from an AI assistant. Grade strictly against the rubric. You do not know which assistant or configuration produced it. ## The user's request / ## Files the assistant was given / ## Answer key (hidden from the assistant) ## The assistant's full written answer <answer>…redacted…</answer> ## Rubric (score each item 0, 0.5 or 1) Reply with JSON only: {"items":[{"id":"R1","score":0|0.5|1,"reason":"<=25 words"}],"false_claims":["…"]} 6. Decide in advance what counts as a pass. Ours, for marketplace candidates: the skill's mean beats baseline, no task falls more than 0.05 below baseline, and any false-claim pattern the skill causes is fixed and re-run. The public skills repo has the result JSON files for each skill in its evals/ folders, including per-run checks, rubric reasons and the frozen-task hash: aicraftbook/aicraftbook-skills . The raw run folders and frozen task files are not in the public repo. For how one skill's results are presented to readers, see the MCP Mechanic page . Limits Everything above ran in Claude Code only, with Sonnet as the agent and Opus as the grader. The first round used Claude Code 2.1.303. The samples are 12 to 15 runs per condition. The checks are regexes, so they can miss a correct answer that uses different wording, or pass a wrong one that happens to match. A combined score near 1.0 on synthetic tasks says the skill keeps its own promise on those tasks. It does not show that the skill helps on your codebase. Most of the useful findings came from reading the false-claim lists by hand, not from the means. This article was drafted with AI assistance (Claude Code) from our project's code and test records, and reviewed and edited by Tim S before publishing.

title: What if a programming language asked 'What do you intend?' instead of 'How?'
author: Art
summary: Most programming languages ask you a question before you've even started: How? How do I allocate this window? How do I register this callback? How do I keep the button and the label in sync? How do I build, package, sign and ship it? I've been building a language that asks something else first: What do you intend? It's called ForgeIL , short for Intention Language. It's part of Forge4D , an open-source project I've been working on, and it's very much early-stage. Let me show you what I mean, and then I'd really like to hear where you think it's wrong. Describing instead of instructing Say you want a small app: a window, a greeting, a button. When the button is pressed, the greeting changes. That sentence is already the whole program. Everything else is translation. In ForgeIL you write down what is there: Window { id : mainWindow title : " Hello " size : 480 , 320 VBoxContainer { anchors : left | top | right | bottom Label { id : greeting text : " Hello, Forge! " } Button { id : btnHello text : " Say hello " } } } And you write down what should happen: on btnHello . clicked () { greeting . text = " Hello again! " } No framework imports, no subclassing, no lifecycle methods, no listener wiring. You describe the structure and the reaction; a runtime handles the how. Two halves, on purpose ForgeIL consists of two deliberately different languages: Half Answers File Example SML (Simple Markup Language) What is there? .sml Button { id: save text: "Save" } SMS (Simple Multiplatform Script) What should happen? .sms on save.clicked() { … } SML has no logic at all: no loops, no conditions, no variables. Only things and their properties. SMS handles behaviour: variables, functions, decisions, and above all events. Its syntax is small and borrows from Kotlin. A screen is usually a pair of files with the same name, main.sml and main.sms , and the runtime wires them together by id. Why not one language? Structure changes slowly, behaviour changes often. A designer can rearrange the whole layout without touching a line of script, as long as the ids stay. Structure can be checked before anything runs. An unknown property is a warning, not a crash. Regular structure is easy for machines to write. SML is so uniform that an AI model can generate it reliably. That's by design, and it's the part I'm most curious about (more below). Behaviour stays small. The script doesn't build the UI, so it only contains actual logic. A typical screen is a few dozen lines. What the runtime does You don't compile, link or package by hand while developing. The Forge Runner builds the native UI from SML (macOS, Linux, Android) and compiles SMS straight to native machine code via LLVM. No VM, no garbage collector. When the app is ready, the same project builds into a .app or .apk with the runner inside. Honest status This is an early edition. Part I of the accompanying book is complete and every example in it runs in the current runner. While writing Part III, I found parts of SMS that the native compiler doesn't handle correctly yet, so I'm fixing the compiler first and the chapters on SML and SMS will follow. I'd rather tell you that now than have you find out. It's all GPL 3.0 or later, with a commercial license for companies that only want to take, close and sell. Prior art, and what's different "Intention" as a programming concept isn't new. Charles Simonyi's Intentional Programming at Microsoft Research in the 90s stored programs as trees of intentions, independent of syntax. The difference I'm betting on is that today an AI can do the translation from intent to implementation, and that a strict, small, regular language gives that AI (and the human) something precise to target, instead of free-form prompts. Where I'd love your opinion Is a hard split between structure (no logic) and behaviour a feature or a limitation? Where did similar splits hurt you (think XAML, QML, HTML and JS)? If AI writes more and more code, should we design languages for being reliably generated (small, regular, checkable) rather than for human cleverness? Is "native, no GC" the right call for UI scripting, or an unnecessary constraint? What would make you try something like this? What would make you close the tab?
